documents.title: Flame Spread Over Thin and Thick Fuels in Microgravity: Results from the BASS Investigation
documents.authors: Olson, S. L., Ferkul, P. V., Tien, J. S.
documents.publication: Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, Vol. 35, Issue 3, pp. 2631-2638

passages.text: For cast PMMA slabs (10 mm thick) tested in the Microgravity Science Glovebox at 21% O2 and 101.3 kPa, the concurrent flame spread rate was measured at 1.85 ± 0.08 mm/s under a forced concurrent airflow of 5.0 cm/s.

In microgravity, unlike terrestrial buoyant flames, low forced flow velocities (below ~2 cm/s) limit oxygen transport to the reaction sheet via diffusion alone, driving thick solid flames toward radiative extinction. Increasing flow velocity between 2 cm/s and 10 cm/s enhances flame spread by replenishing oxidizer faster than convective cooling can quench the base.

Simplified de Ris thermal flame spread models overestimate microgravity spread velocity by 35-45% because they omit solid-phase surface radiative losses, which become dominant when buoyant gas velocity is absent.

documents.title: Extinction of Flame Spread Over Fabric Samples in Microgravity
documents.authors: Ferkul, P. V., Olson, S. L.

passages.text: Cotton-fiberglass blend (Sibal) fabric exposed to 18% O2 at 98.5 kPa achieved steady flame spread at 2.40 mm/s with 2.5 cm/s flow, but exhibited abrupt radiative extinction when the flow speed was stepped down below 1.1 cm/s.

At very low ventilation speeds, the heat release rate per unit flame area drops below the rate of gas and surface radiative heat loss, establishing a lower-bound flammability limit unique to microgravity environments.

documents.title: Structure and Extinction of Nonpremixed Methane Flames in Microgravity
documents.authors: Sunderland, P. B., Urban, D. L., Stocker, D. P., Chao, B. H.

passages.text: Methane laminar diffusion flames in CIR with 30% O2 and quiescent flow displayed a maximum visible flame width of 26.4 mm and peak soot volume fraction of 2.8 ppm, remaining stable down to a critical fuel mass flow rate of 14.8 mg/s.

Without buoyant acceleration, gaseous residence times in the flame zone increase by nearly an order of magnitude, resulting in distinct chemical kinetics pathways and enhanced radiative emission per mole of fuel consumed.

documents.title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment: Saffire-I and Saffire-II Results
documents.authors: Urban, D. L., Ruff, G. A., Ferkul, P. V., Olson, S. L., Fernandez-Pello, C., T'ien, J. S., Torero, J. L.
documents.publication: Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, Vol. 37, Issue 3, pp. 4153-4160

passages.text: In Saffire-I, the 0.4 m x 1.0 m Sibal fabric burned continuously with an average flame spread rate of 5.20 mm/s in a 20.0 cm/s concurrent airflow at 21% O2 and 100.5 kPa, producing a peak radiant heat flux of 11.4 kW/m².

Comparison of Saffire-I large-scale burns with small glovebox samples (BASS) and ground standard NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 demonstrates that flame spread velocity scales nonlinearly with sample width due to lateral preheating and reduced edge heat loss in large geometries.

During Saffire-II sample 4 burns, PMMA strips in 15 cm/s flow generated smoke with peak optical density of 0.82 m⁻¹ and steady flame spread of 3.10 mm/s, demonstrating persistent smoke accumulation in enclosed spacecraft ducts.

documents.title: Warm and Cool Flame Droplet Extinction in Microgravity
documents.authors: Nayagam, V., Dietrich, D. L., Ferkul, P. V., Hicks, M. C., Williams, F. A.
documents.publication: Combustion and Flame, Vol. 162, Issue 5, pp. 2140-2147

passages.section: Droplet Burning Rate and Second-Stage Combustion
passages.text: Isolated n-heptane droplets in CIR microgravity displayed an initial burning rate constant K = 0.58 mm²/s, underwent hot flame extinction at diameter 1.42 mm, and then sustained an invisible cool flame burning regime for 14.5 seconds.

The discovery of microgravity cool flames indicates that chemical reaction and fuel consumption can persist at temperatures below 800 K without visible radiation, presenting a stealth hazard where standard optical sensors would register flame extinction while combustion continues.

documents.title: Concurrent Flame Spread Over Thick Cylindrical Fuels in Microgravity
documents.authors: Bhattacharjee, S., Paolini, C., Takahashi, S., Wakai, K.
documents.publication: AIAA Propulsion and Energy Forum, AIAA 2017-3852

passages.text: In the SLICES MSG experiments, cylindrical HDPE fuel rods burning in 10 cm/s concurrent airflow exhibited a steady flame spread velocity of 1.25 mm/s at 21% O2.

Scaling computations indicate that for thick cylindrical geometries, the maximum concurrent spread rate occurs near 15 cm/s airflow; at speeds above 35 cm/s, convective blow-off extinction is projected to dominate.
